newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian light low-sulphur crudes given a boost.
newsitem.headline: Asian light low-sulphur crudes given a boost.

text.p: Strong demand to produce middle distillate oil products ahead of the fourth quarter is giving light sweet crude oil a seasonal boost.

But sharp production cutbacks at Australia's Cossack field, which produces light sweet crude, and the strength of Brent crude oil are sparking additional demand for regional light grades, traders said on Friday.
A surge in the value of Brent has closed the arbitrage opportunity for Asian buyers to buy West African crudes, which often compete with regional light grades, traders said.
"There is no give because dated Brent means West African crudes can't come into the region. Once we see those coming, sellers can be more concessionary," one trader said.
Australia's light sweet Cossack crude was trading at a differential of minus 90 cents per barrel in late July for August and September liftings. It is now assessed around minus 40 cents.
Production has been erratic and at times cut back to around 50,000 barrels per day (bpd) from a more usual 115,000-120,000 bpd owing to technical problems exporting associated gas into a gas grid.
Cutbacks are expected to continue until October while repair work is carried out, said Woodside Petroleum Ltd, a partner in the field.

The regional benchmark light sweet crude, Malaysia's Tapis, is currently assessed at a premium of 50 to 65 cents per barrel. While its premium had been mostly steady this month, its outright price has firmed strongly to around $21.50 per barrel on Friday from $20.20 per barrel on August 1.
"Right now the grades here are going to be popular because they are at lower prices than those out of the region," a trader at a major oil compnay said.

By comparison, dated Brent, which is used as the base price for many West African crude trades, is valued at $21.00 in Europe. That does not leave enough room to add freight costs and still compete on price with regional grades, traders said.
Light sweet grades, light weight and with a low sulphur content, are easier for refineries to process into light distillates and, more important, middle distillates.
The middle distillates, like kerosene and gas oil, are in greater demand heading into the winter from north Asian countries as they prepare for the colder season.
"Economics in refineries are swinging to maximum light sweet input at the expense of heavy sweet to maximize distillates output," one trader said.
The added incentive for refiners is that kerosene prices in Asia have surged in recent weeks.
Singapore market prices for jet/kerosene surged 18 percent to $28.60 per barrel by Thursday from $24.15 on July 9.

The fourth-quarter jet/kerosene crack against the popular Dubai crude oil, often used by refiners to lock in a profit margin, has ballooned by $3.00 to $12.00 per barrel in the last month, reflecting the demand for jet/kerosene.
On the flip side of the crude equation, regional medium grades have suffered in recent weeks as demand for the slightly heavier and slightly more sour grades waned.
China was only a moderate buyer in August of Indonesia's benchmark Minas grade and demand from Japanese utilities, traditonally a strong buyers, was lower than had been expected.
Minas prices fell to less than $19.00 per barrel for August and September barrels from more than $20.00 in July. Its market differential fell to a 70-cent discount from a 45 cent premium.

"Everyone predicted a big consumption by Japanese utilities and refineries and everyone took long positions in August deliveries. Finally they found they were wrong. Many availabilities came into the market which filled the market with more supply than the market had expected," one trader said.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
